In our experiments, our RNN system demonstrated superior performance, outperforming existing competitors by a significant margin on both precision and energy efficiency metrics. Our findings show that our method can accurately complete tasks at a fraction of the energy required by conventional techniques, achieving a 95% energy savings in our best-case scenario.

This research investigates the composition and characteristics of spin-aligned strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at high temperature, using the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we explored the structure of strange quark stars in this context. When the temperature reaches the chiral transition temperature, the influence of the magnetic field on strange quark matter's phase transition is examined. Additionally, we examined the impact of temperature and magnetic field on the quark star's mass and radius.

In our study, we've introduced three new concepts: Hamiltonian pair-ideals within a particular class of graphs, tintable graphs, and bihamiltonian circuits. We've established a categorical equivalence between these concepts and the presence of a specific type of pairing structure in a set of graphs. This equivalence allows us to prove the existence of a particular type of pairing structure in bihamiltonian circuits. We've also explored the relationships between these concepts and other established concepts in graph theory, including the absence of a Hamiltonian path and the absence of a factor of a certain degree. Additionally, we've identified new criteria for a cubic graph to have a Hamiltonian circuit, as well as new criteria for the existence of a pairing structure in certain types of graphs.

This research focuses on analyzing the underlying structure of a set of polynomials in variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ with the property that for any prime characteristic $p$, the coefficients of the polynomials are not divisible by $p$. It's established that this condition is equivalent to a specific geometric constraint related to hyperplanes in a modified arrangement, specifically requiring that the constraint be non-empty when changing the characteristic of the coefficients. A key contribution of this research is identifying a specific set of polynomials meeting the initial condition for any prime characteristic, and a key open question remains finding a finite set of arrangements for which the associated prime characteristic condition cannot be expressed using a finite set of constraints.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering rules in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls associated with each part of the application's code and create a precise filtering protocol to prevent unauthorized access. This method is designed to work with existing virtualization technologies and can be applied to various programming languages. A practical implementation of Timeloops is also presented, along with the results of a comparative performance test showing that it has a negligible impact on the application's performance.

This research investigates how the addition of a dark sector that includes a pseudo-Goldstone boson (pGB) mediates interaction between two Higgs fields, within the context of a modified Standard Model. We discover that a dark sector that contains a pGB particle is naturally produced in the early universe and results in the present-day universe being composed of pGB dark matter. This occurrence is heavily influenced by the value of the $B-L$ charge of the dark sector's smallest representation, as it determines the rate at which the pGB field decays. Additionally, we find that a dark sector with a charge of $1$ or $2$ enables the pGB to possess a long enough lifespan to be considered a stable component of the universe. We also analyze the model's predictions in relation to the Large Hadron Collider's ability to detect the pGB, as well as the potential for it to be produced in a future electron-positron collider. We find that in the event that the pGB's lifespan is short enough, the LHC would be capable of detecting it with a probability of around $10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we discover that in the event that the pGB's lifespan is lengthy enough, it may be produced in a future electron-positron collider at a rate that is heavily dependent on the value of the $B-L$ charge of the dark sector's smallest representation.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are described by a lattice-based density, enabling efficient computation of predicted targets. The proposed method is particularly beneficial for applications involving sensor management, as it yields optimized sensing strategies by valuing the identification of high-density target regions. The approach is rigorously evaluated against more lax filtering methods, utilizing both simulated and real data in its assessment.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that incorporates an internal nonhomogeneous degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame.

The success of soccer teams is often determined by small moments in key games, and they face significant challenges in assessing risks and seizing opportunities. Human coaches leverage their experience and intuition to make strategic decisions, but it is difficult to systematically analyze their effectiveness. We explore the potential of using deep reinforcement learning to develop a strategic approach for soccer teams by modeling the traditional 4-3-3 and 4-4-2 formations. Our model learns the advantages and disadvantages of various actions and their associated risks, and we evaluate its performance against human-coached teams in simulated games. Our analysis reveals that the model can excel in certain situations and even rival human-coached teams, while in other situations it may struggle to keep up. Furthermore, we discover that our model can learn specific strategies for situations like defending a lead or overcoming a goal deficit, and even adapt to different game phases, including half-time and extra time.

High-resolution subsurface imaging can be achieved through waveform inversion, a leading technique that maps source wavefield recordings to subsurface properties. However, traditional waveform inversion is hampered by high nonlinearity, leading to stagnation and inaccurate results. A hybrid method combines wavefield simulations and data misfit calculations using machine learning models, offering a more efficient alternative. Two expansions of this technique are explored: expanded source waveform inversion, which uses multiple sources to map simulated wavefields to properties, and time-domain expanded source waveform inversion, which involves solving a system of linear equations using simulated wavefields from multiple sources. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of these approaches in realistic scenarios.

We investigate the interaction of quantum field with quantized electromagnetic fields in spatially asymmetric cavities. Our analysis reveals that the quantum effects can cause a deviation from optical symmetry. This deviation can be quantified using Wigner function phase-space averages, which show that the quantum influence dominates classical behavior in asymmetric cavities. Our findings are validated using two methods: first, by directly analyzing the field's correlation functions within the cavity, and second, by examining the cavity's scattering matrix. Our research also demonstrates that quantum compression induces optical asymmetry, and this effect can be utilized to develop novel diode-based optical systems.

The Be/X-ray binary neutron star system IGR J19294+1816 underwent a high-flux state in September 2019, and AstroSat was quickly positioned to gather data. Analyzing this data, we identified a key frequency of 0.83 mHz, considered a low-frequency QPO, as well as a characteristic energy of 43.7 keV, attributed to cyclotron emission, both aligning with past observations, and providing valuable insights for future missions like XLIS.

To analyze the dynamics of species competition in a diverse range of environmental scenarios, we've developed a comprehensive statistical physics model that can handle multiple species in a network of interconnected habitats. The model is based on a voter model framework and incorporates elements of competition and colonization to account for the complex interactions between these species. As the model is applied to different numbers of species, we've identified various coexistence patterns, including stable coexistence and cyclic behaviors, as well as the eventual dominance of one species and random species elimination. Our study provides a detailed analysis of the competition-colonation balance in the model, as well as the influence of this balance on the ecosystem's dynamics.

Ancient cultures used sundials for timekeeping, and their legacy continues with modern sundials serving both practical and educational purposes. However, the construction principles and operating guidelines for these historical timekeeping devices are no longer commonly known. To reclaim this forgotten knowledge, a comprehensive online database called the Suryakala-Nusantara platform has been developed, detailing the construction and functioning of sundials using both text and image-based descriptions. Furthermore, the project is exploring the possibility of reviving this ancient technology through community engagement and participatory action research methods.

This paper proposes a integrated data and power transmission network, featuring a central Intellect Reflecting Surface that facilitates efficient bidirectional communication and simultaneous power transmission between devices. This system leverages Full-Duplex technology to enable simultaneous transmission and reception, and utilizes a non-linear power transmission method to increase the bit rate. To optimize performance, a multi-objective optimization problem is formulated and solved through an algorithm based on the DQNA framework. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in maximizing the network's information transmission rate and reducing the interference between devices.

Recently, there is growing interest in the precise control of blood flow in small vessels, driven by the need to develop more effective treatments for stroke. Carotid endarterectomy, a common surgical intervention, involves removing plaque buildup from the neck's internal carotid artery. Although it is generally successful, improving outcomes requires addressing the risk of intracerebral hemorrhage associated with this procedure. Advances in neuroimaging and computational modeling hold promise for better understanding the relationship between blood flow and brain injury. However, achieving this goal requires real-time, precise control of blood flow using LDV technology. This study presents a novel approach to controlling blood flow using a single-point LDV system via a mechanical valve. Experiments conducted in an artificial vessel demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in regulating blood flow velocity and volume. This technology was then integrated with a light source and a signal processor to enable real-time, 2D velocity and volume measurements. This breakthrough has implications for developing closed-loop feedback systems that could improve outcomes in surgical interventions like carotid endarterectomy.

Convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) has long been utilized for determining crystal structure, but accurate analysis is hampered by sample tilt uncertainty, which often results in incorrect crystal symmetry identification due to false positives from double diffraction. A programmable phase disk in a transmission electron microscope can potentially alleviate this issue by incorrectly introducing even-order Laue zones, allowing for distinction between genuine and spurious diffraction patterns based on ring spacing. This concept was tested on various materials, including metals (copper, gold, and silver), a semiconductor (silicon), and a ceramic (aluminum nitride), with the results showing that in some cases, genuine and spurious patterns can be differentiated by examining the ratio of spacings within the zero-order Laue zone. However, this method has limitations and should be employed in conjunction with other methods for complete analysis.

The task of matching unknown users to unidentified chat messages requires predicting an underlying one-to-one mapping. Success in this task has been achieved by training on related tasks, though it remains unclear how the learned models represent the underlying data in relation to the predicted outputs. This study examines the efficacy of pre-trained encoder models in providing sufficient details to support accurate prediction, as well as the benefits of incorporating additional training. Our findings indicate that while models can perform accurately on the related tasks, the representations used are inadequate, and further that additional training yields limited improvements. This is attributed to the constraint of parallel data used for training, which restricts the ability of models to utilize contextual information. As such, future work may explore the application of models trained on larger datasets.

In this research, a novel LiDAR location recognition system called AttDLNet is introduced, focused on identifying locations within a predefined area using 3D point clouds. Unlike existing approaches that rely on limited description languages or draw from limited training datasets, our system utilizes a more extensive set of predefined places to train a robust model. To improve performance, a 3D feature extraction module was developed that combines range-based and surface-based features to provide more comprehensive information about each location. Additionally, an advanced description module was proposed to classify LiDAR scans based on their structural and textual characteristics. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our system excels in comparing LiDAR scans from the same or different locations and outperforms a baseline approach using a state-of-the-art 3D matching algorithm.

Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, but their prices vary substantially, but often do so in a way that's not linear. This research aims to assist cloud providers and streaming services in deciding how to allocate computing resources, both physically and virtually, by developing a linear regression model to forecast transcoding performance. This model can facilitate efficient resource utilization, especially during peak demand, and the researchers also compare the efficiency of different cloud providers using a case study.

We investigate the thermal response of doped graphene sheets to localized heat sources, analyzing the local temperature change as a function of distance and doping level. A notable decrease in temperature is observed near the surface, characterized by a finite temperature shield that can be optimized through doping. The optimal doping level is found to be inversely proportional to the square root of the conductivity and directly proportional to the fourth root of the specific heat capacity of the material. A dimensional analysis yields a dimensionless parameter representing the efficiency of heat reduction, which can be optimized through doping. The results are validated using three different methods, including analytical models, numerical simulations with heat transfer equations, and molecular dynamics simulations. The proposed framework is applicable to various types of nanostructures and provides a foundation for exploring the thermal shielding capabilities of these materials through doping.

Continuous speech generates endless possibilities, making it challenging to develop practical applications. To address this issue, many approaches focus on limited contexts, but these systems often struggle to generalize well. In contrast, our proposed MaskedSpeech model leverages contextual information from a limited context and uses a masking strategy to avoid predicting unnecessary information. During training, it uses both partial and full sentence masks to learn from various patterns, and our experiments show that MaskedSpeech achieves state-of-the-art performance on various tasks, including sentence generation, language modeling, and response generation.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

Q-ball studies in a single charge system are common, yet the theory allows for multiple charge configurations. In this research, we examine how coexistence of charges affects the stability of Q-balls. To achieve this, we first derive a general inequality applicable to any charge setup, guaranteeing the stability of Q-balls when their total energy meets certain criteria. This is then applied to a specific case involving the intersection of two symmetries, a scenario previously unexplored in detail. By analyzing the simplest scalar field model, we demonstrate that instability in these multi-charge configurations can arise at both the zero and non-zero temperature. Furthermore, we identify a critical parameter $\kappa$ that determines the stability of Q-balls, and show that it can be influenced by the number of charges and the temperature. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings for collaboration and conflict between different symmetries within a multi-charge system.

We investigated a cyclic universe containing holographic dark energy with different infrared cutoffs, excluding the Big Rip singularity. The study reveals that, in the absence of interaction between the cosmos sectors, the HDE model using the Hubble radius cutoff behaves like a cosmological constant within cyclic universes. Furthermore, we discovered that cyclic universality can be achieved even with an interacting HDE model, provided that the interaction rate satisfies a specific relationship. A numerical method was employed to examine the dynamical evolution of the universe, and our findings indicate that cyclic universes can be proficiently described through a suitable parameterization.

Gnutzmann and Smilansky previously developed a formula for the bond scattering matrix of a graph using a Hermitian matrix, but their method only applied to unique, combined reflections at the graph's nodes. In this study, we expand on the Gnutzmann-Smilansky formula by incorporating arbitrary reflection matrices at the nodes, thereby significantly enhancing its applicability. We demonstrate this by deriving a general formula for the bond scattering matrix of a graph, even with non-uniquely combined reflections at the nodes. This results in a novel, concise method for calculating the bond scattering matrix. To effectively utilize this approach, the underlying graph's Hermitian matrix must be a normalized Laplacian matrix. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the enhanced formula and the recent breakthrough by Bary-Sherer, Guionnet, and Shlosman, also deriving a straightforward, direct proof.

We derive new conclusions regarding the properties of a particular set of non-commutative algebras, which are in the form of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ as a extension of $\mathbb{Q}$. Specifically, we determine key characteristics of the central quotient of these algebras' adjoint automorphism group. Notably, we obtain conditions under which this quotient has a defined product operation and when it satisfies the requirements of a non-archimedean local field. These conditions are met if a certain subgroup of the algebra's adjoin automorphism group exhibits characteristics similar to those of the cyclotomic Camille Pisot group while also meeting the requirements for being a non-archimedean local field. These results can be applied to limit cases of the algebra $\mathbb{Q}_p(\xi_N)$, which is defined by a complex Nth root $\xi_N$ of unity. Conclusions regarding the properties of its subalgebras can be deduced from our main conclusions regarding the properties of $\mathbb{Q}_p(\xi_N)$.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on specific signatures, often requiring a thorough understanding of existing decay processes. By examining specific decay modes of certain particles, researchers can pinpoint a potential neutral long-lived particle by identifying gaps in current decay data. This paper focuses on searching for a specific type of particle, called a axion-like particle, by analyzing decay patterns of certain particles that have collided with photons and muons. By using existing data from the Belle II experiment and incorporating theoretical predictions about the particle's possible decay, researchers can determine the most effective ways to identify the particle's presence. By exploring various scenarios based on different experimental conditions and assumptions about the particle's properties, researchers can identify the most promising approaches to detecting the particle, with some methods offering the potential to identify the particle even if it doesn't fit the expected decay pattern.

This paper offers an evaluation of the effectiveness of contextualized language frameworks in detecting semantic alterations, a critical capability for ensuring the trustworthiness of machine translation platforms. Semantic alterations refer to intentional changes made to original text for malicious purposes, such as spreading false information or financial scams. To assess the contextualized language frameworks, we utilized a dataset containing true and false versions of text, where the false versions were created by intentionally making semantic alterations to the original content. We analyzed the performance of multiple contextualized language frameworks, including BERT, ALBERT, and RoBERTa, in identifying semantic alterations across five different languages. The evaluation was conducted using various models and was expanded to cover 20 different languages. The results showed that contextualized language frameworks can achieve high accuracy rates in detecting semantic alterations across different languages. Additionally, we observed that smaller models like BERT and larger models like ALBERT and RoBERTa achieve similar accuracy levels, and that contextualized language frameworks perform better when evaluating semantic alterations at the sentence level rather than the word level.

Accurate measurements of a massive quasar's spin can be derived from the relationship between the quasar's accretion disk and its maximum emission radius, using geometric methods that take into account an inclination angle. Recent research using this approach has yielded results for two quasars: OLS103433+040146, with a spin of 0.83, and OLS025347+000 Five, with a spin of 0.94. These high spin rates are unexpected, given the generally accepted theory that quasars with high accretion rates will have rapid disk evolution, resulting in decreased spin rates over time. Additionally, the predicted masses of these quasars, based on their luminosity and accretion rate, are extremely large, in the range of billion solar masses. The most surprising finding, however, is the implication that these quasars could have ultralight scalar field particles with masses in the range of 10^-20-10^-19 GeV, potentially capable of losing mass through a process called superradiance. The development of more accurate methods for measuring quasar spins will be crucial in validating or disproving these findings using observational data.

A distinctive feature of neural tissue development is the interkinetic nuclear migration of cells between opposite poles of the tissue. This process is driven by a rhythmic interaction between two opposing forces: a spindle-like astrotactically guided movement and a more direct, less organized pull. Researchers previously believed these forces acted in perfect harmony, but using high-speed, long-term imaging and advanced mathematical models in the zebrafish retina, they now found that this process is actually overcorrected and subject to random fluctuations. As a result, the nuclear movement exhibits a characteristic dispersal similar to that seen at the edge of a chaotic mixing zone. This newly understood mechanism of nuclear movement may be a critical factor in achieving the complex spatial arrangements necessary for proper brain function.

In various imaging applications like video compression and color image demosaicing, a specific type of image processing problem needs to be solved, involving the restoration of full-resolution images from reduced and interpolated data. The problem can be framed as a linear model with unknown underlying structure, typically addressed with traditional minimum-variation methods. However, these methods often result in over-smoothing, especially in areas with high intensity gradients. Recently, a more effective approach based on source separation has been proposed, yielding better compression algorithms and improved color images. This work builds on that concept, refining the source separation algorithm to handle external noise and non-uniformly spaced samples, resulting in more accurate and robust compression algorithms and color image demosaicing techniques.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active liquids in scenarios where particles are inextricably linked and cannot move relative to each other. This framework is relevant to dimensions greater than two, where there is no rearrangement of particles as the system scales. A precise set of hydrodynamic equations has been created, accounting for the impact of particle connectivity on both the hydrodynamic regime and an underlying glassy phase that influences the active dynamics. Our models predict that connectivity significantly reduces the viscosity and stresses within the liquid, while also increasing the long-range algebraic decay of fluctuations. This means that connectivity has a non-neighborhood effect on polar active liquids in dimensions greater than two.

The analysis of scholarly cooperation networks has long been observed to yield beneficial outcomes for researchers, enabling them to track the evolution of collaborations and identify potential opportunities. While they've been extensively studied in the past, our research proposes a novel method for evaluating the strength of collaborations by considering the co-authorship of future research papers. We've applied this approach to two separate datasets, and our results show a statistically significant correlation between strong collaborations and future cooperative efforts. Furthermore, we've developed a metric to quantify the potential for future cooperation, and through practical applications, we've been able to pinpoint specific researchers who are likely to engage in cooperative activities. Our research is the first of its kind to explore the concept of temporal complexity in scholarly cooperation networks, and we believe our results have significant implications for entities seeking to establish strategic collaborations.

A novel kind of extraordinary van Hove singularity has recently been identified in pseudogapped alloys, which occurs when a full symmetry point on the Fermi surface experiences a highly anomalous feature due to the intersection of two disjoint continuous Fermi surfaces. This phenomenon was initially thought to require a specific "Fermi sea" shape, as seen in the Shubnikov de Haas effect, but researchers have now discovered that it can arise more generally, even if the Fermi surface appears normal vis-a-vis angular-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. A new theoretical framework has been developed to explain the conditions necessary for creating these singularities, which can lead to exceptionally high peak heights in the density of states and result in unusual electronic properties, such as large positive magnetization and non-trivial Chern number. To realize these singularities, the researchers propose using 5d transition metals, which naturally form pseudogaps due to their large hybridization, but can also produce the desired van Hove singularities with the right combination of alloying and external pressure.

The Aberdeen Tunnel facility holds significant potential for studying spallation neutrons utilizing a 800 MeV proton beam. However, the presence of concrete and rock within the tunnel may substantially impact neutron measurements. To accurately assess this, a device has been developed to monitor fast neutron flux at multiple points within the tunnel's center. This device consists of six layered detectors, each composed of a combination of plastic scintillator and metallic trackers. It allows for simultaneous determination of neutron flux and background measurement, as well as identification and exclusion of protons and muons. Given its ability to handle high intensities and fast neutron pulses, this device is well-suited for infilling missing data points in the Aberdeen tunnel's neutron flux map.

The Tepper Institutional Research Fund has allocated resources for a diverse range of projects, with a common goal of enhancing the university's national and international reputation through innovative research initiatives. The assessment will identify the effectiveness of these projects in achieving their objectives and gathering data on their impact. 

To determine the outcome of these initiatives, a comprehensive evaluation of their success will be conducted. This examination will include:

1. Converting research outcomes into tangible metrics (e.g., citation counts, publication rankings, funding secured)
2. Reviewing and validating data on research outputs with the Tepper School's key stakeholders
3. Analyzing and interpreting research metrics in relation to global benchmarks and best practices
4. Identifying areas for improvement and potential areas for innovation in research initiatives

Additionally, the assessment will provide a detailed report highlighting the achievements of the Tepper School in various categories, including but not limited to, faculty expertise, research focus areas, and industry partnerships. 

For the purpose of this study, the following research targets have been selected:

1. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
2. Data Science and Analytics
3. Digital Transformation
4. Energy and Natural Resources
5. Financial Technology
6. Global Supply Chain
7. Healthcare
8. Innovation and Entrepreneurship
9. Cyber Physical Systems
10. Sustainable Business

These targets were chosen based on their relevance to global industry demands and the potential for the Tepper School to leverage them in various areas, including but not limited to, developing

The growth of Remote Work has increased the demand for automated data entry solutions, and one potential application is the extraction of identity documents. This project showcases a mark-up language (XML) structure for storing Indonesian identity documents containing personal information, address, and identification numbers. Additionally, it highlights an XML-based structure for Indonesian passport information. Our research focuses on developing an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline to automatically extract the contents of Indonesian identity documents, including passports, using a combination of the Tesseract-OCR and spaCy techniques. Evaluation of the pipeline revealed a high accuracy rate of 93.5% for extracting Indonesian identity document contents.

Quantum harmonic oscillators have traditionally been comprehensively analyzed, 
but the implementation of damping and propulsion within this context remains 
an area of ongoing research. In our study, we've developed a numerical approach 
to determining the time-dependent propagation of a quantum harmonic oscillator 
subject to damping and propulsion by mapping the time-dependent Schrödinger 
equation into Ising types of models. Our proposed method involves two distinct 
Monte Carlo strategies. Firstly, in the 'operator insertion' method, we've 
adapted the time-dependent propeller harmonic oscillator wavefunction by inserting 
quantum operators within the path integral formulation. In the'stochastic 
evolution' method, we've modeled the time-dependent Schrödinger equation as 
an iterative stochastic process. Both methods yield accurate results when 
compared to an exact quantum harmonic oscillator wavefunction calculator for 
a Propeller-Harmonic-Oscillator in various scenarios. In particular, our study 
shows that the time-dependent propagation of this harmonic oscillator can be 
precisely modeled over several oscillations even with a relatively small number 
of path integral time slices. Additionally, our research highlights the 
advantages of using the operator insertion method which exhibits better scaling 
with increased numbers of division points.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect, or YORP for short, is a phenomenon that affects asteroids by generating a torque due to solar radiation. This force is minimal yet sufficient to cause long-term changes in an asteroid's rotation rate. As solar radiation is absorbed and re-emitted, it creates a imbalance that results in the transfer of momentum to the asteroid. This force is only significant for smaller asteroids with dimensions in the hundreds of meters range. Research has indicated that three such asteroids, (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, all with diameters of approximately one kilometer, are spinning down at a notable rate. Studies have attempted to model the YORP influence on these asteroids, utilizing their shapes, reflection coefficients, and orbital paths to calculate the impact. The YORP values calculated for (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos were found to be 1.4 x 10^-3 deg/day, 2.5 x 10^-3 deg/day, and 1.1 x 10^-3 deg/day respectively. These models also predicted the initial rotation speeds of these asteroids, spin-down times, and the YORP strengths required to achieve their current states.

The rise of social networks has altered the conventional understanding of computer network dynamics. Users on Instagram, for example, form a complex network that evolves quickly in response to external stimuli. This study focuses on the discussions of Canadians sparked by the country's federal election in 2019, utilizing a large dataset of over 10 million posts and their corresponding comments. From a network perspective, analysis reveals the rapid formation of dense communities within the Instagram network, with members actively engaging in reciprocal interactions and sharing content that attracts numerous comments. However, this study also reveals the presence of influential spreaders who play a crucial role in disseminating information throughout the network, with a smaller group of super spreaders responsible for a significant portion of content dissemination. Finally, this study investigates the temporal characteristics of the Instagram network, finding that it exhibits non-linear behavior in response to external stimuli and follows a specific pattern in its development.

We show that any collection of surface homeomorphisms that is bound in the Rottner-Misiurewicz sense does not have compact subsets within the Roelcke topology. This is demonstrated by establishing that the product action of a collection of surface homeomorphisms on the Cantor space contains numerous homeomorphism types.

The amount of stellar rotation rates known for M-dwarfs is relatively low compared to other spectral types, which presents a challenge in modeling M-dwarf activity. The goal of this research is to establish a method for determining the stellar characteristics, such as mass, metal content, and surface gravity, for M-dwarfs with high accuracy. This, in turn, will enable a more precise assessment of the stellar properties of M-dwarfs in the Galactic Planet Survey (GPS) and the California Planet Survey (CPS). By examining a sample of 45 M-dwarfs with spectrophotometric masses between 0.25 M$_{\odot}$ and 0.60 M$_{\odot}$, this study develops an empirical approach to estimating the fundamental properties of these stars. The key findings include a precise determination of the metal content with an accuracy of $\pm$0.05 dex for the majority of the M-dwarfs analyzed, a relatively low scatter of 0.09 dex among the calculated surface gravities, and a range of masses that aligns well with previous measurements. However, it was also discovered that several of the M-dwarfs examined displayed anomalous spectral features which could potentially lead to inaccurately estimated stellar characteristics and active star-disc interactions which could result in inaccurately calculated planetary system parameters.

A novel 2D electrostatic metastructure is proposed, exhibiting a unique capability to steer line waves in two distinct directions via a tightly coupled resonant cavity. The design's behavior can be adjusted to suit different applications, either guiding confined line waves, similar to those in optical fiber, or a wider waveguide mode suitable for electromagnetic propagation. To control the direction of wave guiding, a tight resonance between two identical cavity parts is crucial. The proposed design is analyzed for both rectangular and triangular forms of the metastructure, with triangular showing better wide-sense reciprocity. A simple method is also introduced for calculating the impedance of the dual metastructure. Finally, a triangular dual metastructure is used for a 1.55μm optical communication system, demonstrating the scattering parameters' good agreement with simulation predictions.

A key issue in studying the complexity of tuple-generating functions and fixpoint queries is the presence of self-referential links between variables. To address this, we're exploring the categorical distribution of first-order logic with self-referential links, considering the entire category of presheaves on a specific base category. Initially, we're focusing on a restricted subclass of presheaves characterized by disjoint cyclic associations. Within this context, we can accurately analyze the complexity of conjunctive queries with self-links. Conversely, most complex queries with self-links exhibit complex patterns that render their complexity difficult to analyze. To tackle this challenge, we can apply a novel approach, combining category theory with database complexity analysis. By analyzing a sample query with self-links, we can decompose it into more manageable components, utilizing both category theoretical and traditional methods. Finally, we can express the complexity of such queries using a combination of category theoretical and logical parameters.

We aim to establish a connection between finite and infinite sequences through the concept of executable functions. We begin by defining executable functions for finite sequences, which can be seen as instructions for a two-symbol automaton to generate those sequences. We then determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for a sequence to be able of being generated by some executable function. This involves recognizing that any finite sequence can be generated by an executable function, as it is simply a specific type of infinite sequence with a significant pattern of zeros towards the end. We also find that the condition of being sequentially productive is both necessary and sufficient for an infinite sequence to be able to be generated by some executable function. This means that any sequence meeting this condition will eventually have patterns of the form $01$* repeated indefinitely, allowing it to be generated by an executable function. We discuss how this condition is related to other definitions found in literature and we also show the connection between executable functions and other types of functions like continuous and continuous-within functions. We end by exploring some basic properties of executable functions for infinite sequences, such as their uniqueness and their relationship with the sequences' underlying structure.

Using the LHCb experimental data, available information on $B \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays is analyzed based on event yield measurements. A statistical approach is employed to interpret the results in terms of physical parameters, including the branching ratio of $B \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays. Our analysis reveals the branching ratio to be in the range $2.42 \times 10^{-7}$ to $4.48 \times 10^{-7}$, with uncertainty influenced by experimental errors and theoretical assumptions about hadron characteristics.

In systems with multiple coexisting phases, where the thermodynamic properties are influenced by more than one variable, a fundamental challenge exists in identifying hidden modes of behavior. A new statistical mechanical approach has been developed for inhomogeneous systems that allows researchers to estimate the number of system degrees of freedom. By applying this method to various models, strong evidence has been found indicating that multiple hidden modes of behavior can exist in models that have already been well-characterized. A key finding reveals that some hidden modes of behavior can be triggered by an external force, contradicting the current understanding that drivers are always external forces that push systems in a specific direction. Instead, pullers are internal forces that attract systems in a particular direction. The proposed framework has significant implications for understanding complex systems that exhibit multiple coexisting phases and it can be applied to various systems in physics, biology, and social sciences.

When working with skewed data, the average absolute deviation (AAD) is a reliable measure of spread. However, traditional estimation methods for the AAD often struggle with skewed data sets. We develop a new bias-corrected estimator for the AAD, drawing from the family of bias-corrected and scaled estimation methods. We investigate the properties of this estimator in relation to the classic method and show that it outperforms the standard estimator through simulation studies. Furthermore, we apply the new estimator in conjunction with the median as a measure of central tendency and find that it performs exceptionally well in handling data sets with skewness.

This research introduces a novel approach to estimating second-order attainable sets in continuous-time systems subject to input constraints. The method is primarily grounded in a type of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation of the variational Hamilton-Jacobi-James-Allen type. Existence and uniqueness of a strong solution to this equation are demonstrated, along with a related theorem confirming the accuracy of the attainable sets calculation. An iterative algorithm is also presented, showcasing its effectiveness through computational examples.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are inherently non-linear and are known to be capable of performing complex functions, but their fundamental ability to produce linear transformations is still unclear. Our research addresses this uncertainty by demonstrating that a single hidden layer with a specific activation function can perform any linear transformation on any dataset, and that this ability is also present in MLPs that have multiple layers. Furthermore, we've discovered that using the same activation function throughout the network leads to overfitting, but alternating between two different activation functions in each layer eliminates this issue. To validate our findings, we've developed a method of analyzing the mathematical properties of MLPs using the monotonic autoencoder framework, and employed it to demonstrate that MLPs can produce any linear transformation, and that this ability is a result of the unique functional representations that are learned by each layer. Additionally, we've discovered that the ability of MLPs to perform non-linear transformations is not a result of the use of non-linear activation functions, but rather to the unique way in which the activations are learned, and that the ability to generalize this capability is dependent on the specific choice of activation functions.

Animacy is an inherent quality of life, reflecting the presence of vital biological processes, which is inherently linked to movement within living beings. Previous research suggests that human ventral temporal cortices are capable of detecting this quality through visual cues presented in static images. It has been proposed that this capability is linked to the activation of a specific neural network focused on identifying biological entities, which is thought to be responsible for the animacy arrangement seen in ventral temporal cortices. However, it remains unclear whether this phenomenon is a result of complex biological perceptions being condensed into a simpler concept, or if it involves the intricate details of biological perceptions themselves. In order to answer this question, we conducted two independent experiments utilizing a range of stimuli, which showed that the animacy arrangement in ventral temporal cortices is indeed a simplified representation of life, separate from the complexities of biological perceptions themselves. Additionally, our findings indicate that this simplified representation is uniquely tied to the cortices in question and the perception of life is most effectively conveyed through the unique combination of features found on the lower body area of the subjects in the images, which is critically responsible for the arrangement seen in ventral temporal cortices.

We establish the quantum unique ergodicity (QUE) result for Hecke-Maass newforms under specific assumptions, expanding on a earlier framework by Brumley-Duke. Additionally, we demonstrate that QUE holds universally for all Landau-Siegel newforms within the same context. Furthermore, our findings extend the previously proven QUE results for GL_2 by Brumley-Duke, for Gamma_2-level-quotients by Brumley-Lawson, and for GL_n by Duke-Liu-Shahahani.

In our proposed approach, we bring together quantum and relational Hoare logic within a comprehensive framework that also explores the concept of forward-looking reasoning. Our key innovation allows us to derive imperative quantum programs using relational semantics, even when considering concurrent programs. At the heart of this is a novel way of addressing concurrent program verification that is more expansive than existing methods. We can express program properties using quantified variables that represent the relationship between program inputs and outputs. This means our framework can handle a wide range of program verification tasks, including verification of concurrent programs with arbitrary unitary operators and anticyclonic linear operators. Our framework can also be seen as a natural extension of the quantum Hoare logic proposed by Jungheinrich and Mislove, as well as the relational Hoare logic proposed by Hahnle and Schmitz.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This study aims to investigate the significant impact of such events on epidemic spread rates by analyzing various transmission models, including basic epidemiological, SIR, SEIR, and proportional intensification models. We theoretically and computationally analyze how a super-spreader event affects the epidemic's basic reproduction number, finding that it raises this critical metric dramatically. As a result, traditional control strategies, which rely on the basic reproduction number, may no longer be effective when a super-sp-spreader event occurs. To mitigate this issue, we propose an advanced transmission model that accounts for the super-spreader event and adapts the basic reproduction number accordingly, providing a mathematical framework for estimating the associated parameters. Computational simulations validate our analytical findings, and we apply our model to analyze the COVID-19 outbreak in China, considering the Liwan super-spreader event that occurred in February 2020.

Let's consider an infinite-dimensional, separable topological vector space, denoted as X, that satisfies certain conditions for being infinitely dimensional over the reals. We establish codiskcyclic collections of operators on X with respect to a specific basis, specifically showing that any collection of bounded linear operators on X, which forms a codiskcyclic collection with respect to this basis, also exhibits cyclicity when restricted to a specific closed subspace of X. This achievement comes as a result of combining two main findings. Firstly, we prove the equivalence of continuous codiskcyclic and cyclic properties for collections of operators on X by utilizing properties of the basis in question. Secondly, we establish the presence of a specific measure space that allows us to draw conclusions about the behavior of these operators.

The procedure for deriving magnetic field properties from observed data, specifically unknown biases present in pre-computed maps, is addressed in this study. We first demonstrate the existence of a systematic bias in pre-computed vector magnetic field maps, then investigate its origin, and ultimately propose a quantitative correction method. The proposed method is applied to data from the Heliospheric Spectral Imaging (HIFI) instrument on board the Solar Orbiter, yielding improved results.

A powerful analytical tool for studying the physics of young star formation has been observed in galaxies across the universe, allowing researchers to investigate the relationships between star formation and the gravitational forces that govern galaxy evolution. By analyzing 18 nearby galaxies using the Hubble Space Telescope's data, this study reveals a universal link between the size of regions producing new star formation and the rate at which galaxies rotate. Interestingly, this connection is stronger in galaxies that are rapidly rotating and have a high rate of star formation. Furthermore, this relationship is found to vary depending on the characteristics of the galaxy, with smaller YSOs associations found in galaxies with high rotation rates and high levels of gas consumption, while larger YSOs associations are found in galaxies with stable gas consumption. Despite being influenced by the characteristics of the galaxy, the size of regions producing new star formation remains a key factor in determining the overall rate of star formation.

We present a new method for calculating the electromagnetic form factor of the charmonium system using lattice quantum chromodynamics. This approach is unusual in that it allows for the calculation of the decay width of a charmonium state into two photons without a direct measurement of the matrix element for this process. Our results for the form factor of the $n=1$ $s$-wave state are consistent with previous studies, and we use them to estimate the decay width of this state into two photons. Additionally, we examine the influence of excited $n=1$ states on the photon spectrum in the decay of the $η_c$ meson. Our findings suggest that lattice simulations at relevant energies may be able to accurately model the photon spectrum in this process.

A critical challenge in developing neural network models lies in addressing the problem of singular Hessian matrices that arise during training with second-order methods. This issue, known as the Hubbard Sign Dilemma, significantly hampers efforts to apply efficient optimization techniques to a range of problems, including large-scale machine learning applications and complex quantum simulations that require the differentiation of energy minimization procedures. To overcome this limitation, researchers have introduced complex-valued neural network architectures that are now being applied to a range of problems, including the study of electronic systems using quantum machine learning, in a paper presented at the 36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022). This approach involves representing spin degrees of freedom as complex rather than binary variables. By utilizing the reimagined hubbard model, a significant reduction in sign errors is achieved, and the models demonstrate improved performance in both training efficiency and accuracy, with a particular advantage being the ability to apply efficient optimization techniques. Additionally, these complex-valied architectures show a greater degree of robustness in relation to initial conditions, a key benefit being the capability to apply efficient optimization techniques directly to the energy minimization procedure, resulting in a substantial increase in performance.

Prime factorization plays a fundamental role in understanding the properties of integers. While the concept of divisibility expresses a qualitative relationship between integers, their unique prime factor structure constitutes the essence of their quantitative nature. Consequently, it is essential to identify the moments of a measure $\mu$ that distinguish the prime factor structure of integers, i.e., the set $\mathbb{Z}$, from that of the reals, i.e., the set $\mathbb{R}$. By correlating the moments of $\mu$ with the function $\rho$, we establish conditions under which the prime factor structure of $\mathbb{Z}$ mimics that of $\mathbb{R}$ or fails to do so. Furthermore, we establish an lower bound for the moment $\mu_{4}(\mathbb{Z})$ and demonstrate that it is finite when using a measure $\mu$ derived from the Dickman $\rho$ function.

Given any non-trivial free group F, a subset A that generates a subgroup, and any monoid mapping φ from A to F, there exists an equivalent mapping ψ from φ(A) to F. Furthermore, the topological entropies of the shifts associated with A and φ(A) are equal, and this result extends to asymptotic complexity by showing that the combinatorial complexity of the shifts associated with A and φ(A) are simultaneously minimized or maximized under the same circumstances as for F. Similarly, if φ is a monoid mapping from A to F, and β is any mapping from the set of basis elements of F to the set of basis elements of G, then the topological entropy and asymptotic complexity of the shifts associated with A and φ(A) remain unchanged.

Machine learning models excel when tasked with drawing from a wealth of labeled data from a specific domain, but struggle with answering questions from unrelated domains. This challenge highlights the limitations of both supervised and self-supervised learning. By leveraging a diverse range of unannotated texts, our proposed method, Retrieval Enhancement for Cross-task Generalization (RECG), enables models to acquire unsupervised cross-generalization capabilities. Our experiment shows that RECG successfully extends the scope of a model's expertise, allowing it to achieve remarkable task generalization results on distantly related tasks. Notably, RECG-fine-tunes the model with only 500 unlabeled texts per task, as opposed to vast amounts of question-answer pairs typically required for fine-tuning. Our result indicates that RECG achieves a significant boost in performance, outperforming a model trained on the full dataset by 5.3% in F1 score, while also demonstrating the effectiveness of RECG across multiple datasets and tasks.

This research introduces the m-ar-K-Fast algorithm for autonomous component analysis in real-time, dynamic, and multivariate systems. Unlike traditional dynamic factor analysis methods that rely on theoretical models for asset pricing and use historical data to estimate their parameters, this new method skips the model formation process. By leveraging high-frequency data and an adaptive, semi-parametric approach, the m-ar-K-Fast algorithm discovers hidden factors, extracts their characteristics, and calculates factor prices within a short-time frame. In a backtest using real data from the S&P 500, the study shows that the m-ar-K-Fast algorithm can identify essential factors, accurately price them, and create portfolios with better performance and lower risk than those from the CapM and 4-Factor models.

This paper offers an all-encompassing examination of requirements engineering approaches in the gaming industry. Despite the economic and social impacts of digital games, developers face considerable challenges in delivering high-quality products on time. To better understand the complexities involved, a thorough analysis of 16 RE approaches was conducted and their applications in the gaming sector were examined. The examination revealed that most RE approaches can be relevant to gaming development, however, few are specifically tailored to address the unique difficulties faced by game developers. A hybrid model combining multiple RE approaches could provide a more comprehensive solution to the unique challenges posed by game development. The research also highlights existing shortfalls in literature and the benefits of further exploring the application of RE methodologies in the gaming industry.

The implementation of differential privacy in deep learning has shown great promise in protecting sensitive information, and our research aims to enhance its performance. To achieve this, we've developed a new approach to hyperparameter tuning for private deep learning. By leveraging a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method and a highly optimized dataset, we've significantly improved the optimization performance without sacrificing much privacy. Our results indicate that this method can achieve up to 86% better test accuracy with minimal loss of differential privacy. Furthermore, we've established that a significant portion of private models trained using standard methods can be matched by our approach at a much lower cost. Our research provides a more efficient and effective way to train private models, and its code is publicly available on GitHub.

A finite classical group G, represented by G(U,V), where U and V comprise angular and dihedral parameters respectively, is examined in this study to identify the boolean structure of its fusion class containing the central element -1. Our analysis shows that this boolean structure is made up of the union of all G-double-cosets, defined by G phi V, with phi being a dementia mapping that classifies the 2-tori in V's orbit.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly impact future cosmological research with its Visible and Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer devices. The authors of this study analyzed how correlated readout noise affects in-flight measurements for the NISP detectors. Initially, the noise is shown to follow a chi-square distribution with a set of degrees of freedom that is directly proportional to the signal intensity. Further investigation reveals that the authors' previous estimation of the signal-to-noise ratio was conservative, thus implying a more substantial scientific instrument performance. Consequently, this study proposes updated and more efficient data processing techniques, including new baseline removal methods and a revised algorithm for detecting and calculating the flux of celestial objects. The authors conclude that these updates will lead to a 10-20 times improvement in the measurement of weak sources and a 4-5 times improvement in the determination of the cosmic void density for NISP's near-infrared band.

Our research utilizes the APOGEE-GALACTIC plane survey to map the metal content of the galactic disk. A two-step protocol for eliminating contaminants allows us to analyze 34,177 unique star targets. By accounting for radial temperature and gravity gradients, we derived the metal content of the disk at various radii. Results indicate the metal content increases with radius, a $0.013\pm 0.003$ dex per kiloparsec trend. However, this relationship may be influenced by stellar populations. A $0.047\pm 0.010$ dex amplitude, sinusoidal pattern in [Fe/H] was detected with a 4.5 gigayear timescale, aligned with the solar neighborhood. Additionally, a $0.21\pm 0.05$ ppm/100 AU trend in [Fe/H] was found with an estimated 1 AU timescale, potentially linked to planetary systems.

This paper analyzes the spread of false information on Chinese social media platforms during the COVID-19 pandemic. A statistical examination of trending trends on the popular Chinese mobile app Weibo revealed the impact of pandemic-related false information on Chinese citizens. In the early stages of the pandemic, the rate of false information spread surpassed true information. However, as public awareness increased, the rate of false information dissemination declined. This decline was attributed to the implementation of stricter moderation policies by Weibo in order to curb the spread of pandemic-related false information. Additionally, the results indicated that public perception of health risks was influenced by the certainty of pandemic-related false information, with a significant correlation found between the two factors. Furthermore, it was observed that Weibo users demonstrated a preference for engaging with pandemic-related false information and true information equally, as evidenced by the similarity in retweet and comment rates.

A novel approach to determining the distances of galaxies within the Fornax cluster has been presented, featuring a comprehensive directory of planetary nebulae for 13 Fornax galaxies participated in the Fornax3D survey. Utilizing data from the K-band, a automated method for distance estimation was developed and applied to the directory's planetary nebulae, resulting in eight independent distance measurements with a small scatter of 0.16, consistent with previous findings from the survey. These methods were compared to traditional methods using bright supernovae and globular cluster luminosities, and were found to be in alignment with the survey's previously determined distance of 19.6 megaparsecs. Additionally, a comparison with the survey's stellar mass-to-surface brightness relation revealed a large scatter, however when the relation was re-examined using planetary nebulae as a secondary method for determining distances, the scatter was significantly reduced, providing further evidence of the planetary nebulae approach's accuracy and utility.

This research paper proposes LifeFlow, a stream processing engine designed to handle regular streams efficiently. Many contemporary applications involve periodic events with fixed time intervals, and thus, there is a common misconception that these events require dynamic systems for optimal performance. In contrast, LifeFlow leverages the predictability of these events to achieve better performance. It is a Java-based engine that utilizes JNI to access native memory for increased speed. LifeFlow outperforms other leading stream processing engines like Apache Flink and Spotify Storm. A no-declaration policy for memory in LifeFlow prevents memory fragmentation, resulting in faster garbage collection and overall higher throughput. Furthermore, LifeFlow supports declarative and imperative programming models, making it a versatile engine. It is an open-source engine that is suite for large-scale, long-duration stream processing tasks.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional semi-Riemannian space, do not exist unless the underlying space has a specific minimum dimension and curvature characteristic.

The unique characteristics of hinge loss, a commonly employed loss function in deep learning for classification, set it apart from other loss functions like softmax cross-entropy. This distinction becomes particularly noticeable when encountering adversarial examples, as the field of training robust models has grown in significance. Despite its importance, the hinge loss's properties remain inadeonlyy understood, mainly because most research focuses on the final achieved results rather than a thorough analysis of its behavior. This paper delves into a comprehensive analysis of hinge loss's performance in various scenarios, including its behavior when encountering different types of data, such as linear samples that are easily classified and non-linear samples that are difficult to classify. Our research also examines how loss function alteration affects the model's performance, particularly its robustness when subjected to different types of noise, such as bounded noise and cut noise. Our findings can provide valuable insights for researchers working on the development of robust deep learning classification models.

A new approach is introduced to stabilize the Navier-Stokes equations using a feedback controller that is based on a slanted boundary controller. This approach can successfully achieve global asymptotic stability for a specific flow configuration near a slanted boundary in a rectangular domain. A key feature of this method is the use of a novel boundary controller that is oriented at an angle compared to the traditional horizontal or vertical boundaries typically employed in similar scenarios.

This research seeks to address the challenge of modeling material microstructure during strain-induced crystallization, a process that influences thermomechanical properties and final product performance. To achieve this, a new approach is presented that incorporates elements from finite element analysis and phase field theory to simulate material deformation and phase transformation. The proposed model leverages the Serret-Higgins kinematics framework to describe material deformation and uses a reduced-Bobylev-Satkin (RBS) function to model non-spherical particles. Additionally, it incorporates an adiabatic normal stress phase field to simulate pressure-dependent phase transitions and account for the impact of crystal formation on material viscosity. A numerical solution is provided for the model's governing equations, along with a simulation of crystallization induced by uniaxial and biaxial tensions. Further, the model's capabilities are demonstrated through simulations of material microstructure development during drawing simulations.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

The traditional approach to teaching robotics through positive reinforcement learning involves marking desired behaviors as rewarding. Yet, achieving expertise in complex tasks often requires learning from negative feedback, i.e., identifying unwanted actions. Until now, providing constructive feedback has been unexplored in robotics due to difficulties in articulating what actions to avoid. This study introduces a novel method of giving constructive feedback for two critical applications: navigating around obstacles in a variety of environments and collecting objects from different locations. By comparing the performance of our procedure to traditional reinforcement learning strategies, we demonstrated that constructive feedback can be as effective as combined positive and negative reinforcement learning, and significantly more effective than negative reinforcement learning alone. Furthermore, we found that constructive feedback enables efficient learning from a single teacher, an impossibility with positive reinforcement learning. These breakthroughs have the potential to substantially expand the scope of tasks that can be learned through reinforcement learning. Due to the innovative use of triangular comparison distances for feedback, our method is also highly adaptable to various sensor technologies.

Continuous phase modulation detection using a non-coherent differential approach
is renowned for its simplicity and robustness. It achieves this by leveraging the
statistical properties of CPM, specifically its high BER performance with a coherently
differentially encoded reference signal. We investigate the underlying reasons for
its beneficial properties and show that increasing the delay per symbol in CAM stages
leads to an optimal balance between two opposing effects - the deterioration of
differential detection performance and the reduction of noise variance. By applying this
insight, we design a modified version of the traditional differential CPM detection
method, called delayed differential detection, and evaluate its performance through
numerical and simulated results. Our findings indicate that carefully selecting the
delay per symbol can result in a significant improvement of up to 5 dB in SNR for some
modulation schemes and formats.

The emergence of gravitational wave detectors like LIGO and VIRGO allows for the observation of binary black hole and neutron star mergers.  However, the ability to locate electrical and radio counterparts of these events relies on the detection of neutrinos.  Neutrino emission is expected from the same highly dynamic processes that form a neutron star's surface in mergers, but hermann-minkowski metrics may hinder efficient detection of such neutrinos.  By analyzing neutrino beaming angles and whether they intersect with Earth, we calculated the probability of detecting such an event with both LIGO and neutrino observatories like ICECUB.  Our results reveal that only a small fraction of such mergers result in detectable neutrinos and that these events typically occur at small angles.  Furthermore, our data shows that about 10% of such mergers with small angles may be detectable with both LIGO and neutrino observatories.  Our results also indicate that in approximately 30% of cases, the Earth will actually block the direction of neutrinos, making them potentially detectable through other methods such as gravitational waves.  Our study is the first of its kind to consider the impact of core-collapse dynamics on the detection of such mergers.  It paves the way for further research into neutrino beaming angles, especially in contexts beyond neutron star mergers.

In the context of Quantum Field Theory, we investigate the quantum potential's impact on the vacuum compressibility of spacetime using thermal systems as an example. By analyzing the thermal pressure and its relationship to the quantum potential, we find that the quantum potential's influence on compressibility cannot be captured by the Casimir effect. Additionally, we show that the quantum potential's impact on compressibility is more significant than the cosmological constant's effect, which is in line with the principles of quantum equidistant theory.

Current deep learning approaches to removing rain from images have made significant progress.
Rain elimination techniques have been particularly effective because they take advantage of the fact that rain formation is a consistent process.
However, these techniques overlook a crucial aspect - the nature of rain - which is not just a visual phenomenon but also indicated by the presence of water droplets in depth.
Existing models fail to account for the intricacies of rain formation and elimination, which is a two-way process, as they only focus on transforming images in the presence of rain.
We propose a novel, reverse approach to rain elimination that considers the two-dimensional image and three-dimensional scene depth as interconnected entities.
Our model is trained to recognize the nature of rain - whether it is falling or has already hit the imaging plane - and to eliminate it in the latter case, as it no longer affects the perceived depth.
For rain that has already hit the imaging plane, our model is tasked with producing a water-free image that maintains the original depth information.
We have tested this approach on a new dataset that includes rain formation and elimination scenarios and compared its performance to existing rain elimination techniques.

Through ongoing research, reward functions are now generated efficiently for multiple goals, thanks to significant advancements in learning from visual feedback.
Despite this progress, creating efficient reward learning in complex environments remains a challenging task.
Our novel approach simplifies this process by introducing a ranking-based framework that utilizes cluster labels in an efficient manner.
By condensing annotation data and bypassing the necessity for explicit policy validation, our framework significantly reduces training time.
Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods in a variety of evaluation scenarios, showing that it is a highly effective solution for reward learning in complex environments.

General relativity, perhaps in conjunction with a cosmological constant, stands alone as a viable theoretical framework to describe gravitational phenomena. However, the absence of a well-defined singularity in black hole holes within this framework forces a reevaluation of the conceptual basis of the singularity theorem. In an attempt to rescue the theorem, an alternative approach is taken here by incorporating a key principle from the holographic hypothesis - namely, the hypothesis that a system's information state can be described through the use of fewer degrees of freedom than those comprising the system's fundamental constituents. It is then shown that this information state description is sufficient to derive the consequences of the singularity theorem, including the inevitability of singularities arising in black hole holes and in an eternally expanding universe. The results obtained point to an intriguing potential for the principles underlying the holographic hypothesis to contribute to a deeper understanding of the singularities characteristic of general relativistic spacetimes.
This study establishes a quantitative relationship between the Q-curvature of a bounded subset of n-dimensional space and its mean and radius.

Our proposal sorts out common knowledge among humans, inferring causal relationships and facts about the world, diverse entities, and everything in between. We present ATOMIC, a comprehensive database mapping instance-level statements to their underlying causal relationships and present various ways it can be put to use in the field of computer vision. ATOMIC is made up of 37 distinct categories, covering nearly 600 areas of life, and is distinguished by its focus on specific, real-world events and their underlying causes. We demonstrate the versatility of ATOMIC by incorporating it into three diverse applications: using machine learning to predict the underlying motivations behind actions, generating detailed scene descriptions, and linking entities within a given context. We hope that by making this extensive resource available to the public, it will become a valuable tool for further advancing computer vision.

As factor-based investment approaches gather momentum on classical platforms, researchers have begun exploring the potential of quantum computing to optimize asset allocation. However, the existing quantum applications face limitations in their feasibility on near-term devices. To address this challenge, this study introduces two novel, efficient strategies for solving the minimum variance portfolio problem, tailored to the risks associated with noisy quantum simulations. One approach, centered on the Monte Carlo method, offers a direct path to portfolio optimization, while the other strategy uses the quantum version of the singular value decomposition to identify risk factors and subsequently derive the minimum variance portfolio. Both methods exhibit superior performance compared to their classical counterparts, with one model displaying an impressive 50% increase in efficiency and the other exhibiting a 15% improvement. Furthermore, these quantum-inspired methods outperform the classical equivalent in asset allocation when simulated on a hybrid quantum-classical system.

To enhance data efficiency for speech recognition, a multi-modal approach has been proposed that utilizes text data in addition to audio. This approach incorporates a multi-modal model that learns from the combined data, but the question remains of how to allocate the focus between the speech and text modes during training. A new method has been introduced that applies a bidirectional attention mechanism, allowing the model to distribute the attention weight evenly between the two modes. Initially, it was observed that this method yields speech models comparable to baseline systems that rely solely on audio data. Furthermore, it was found that when trained in an unsupervised manner on multi-modal data, the model is capable of learning from speech that is poorer quality than what is typically used for training. Additionally, it was discovered that when trained with large datasets, the model is prone to suffering from label noise, resulting in a decline in performance. Nonetheless, this issue is mitigated through the application of diffusion training, which is met with positive results.

In this analysis, areas within a nucleus where the average transverse momentum of the particles emitted is constant are identified. This is done by analyzing datasets from experiments studying the emission of particles when struck with 400 MeV protons, specifically looking at rings of particles emitted at different angles. It was found that in certain areas, particularly those emitting particles at very shallow angles, the average transverse momentum of the particles is zero. This indicates that some areas of the nucleus may have a symmetrical, circular shape. By applying a mathematical transformation to account for the angular momentum of the struck nucleus, areas with zero average transverse momentum were more clearly defined.
