In our research, we explore how Mat\'ern Gaussian functions can be applied to data analyzed on a graph. Originally, these functions are utilized in spatial statistics to model phenomena with varying smoothness levels. By combining them with the methods used for Gaussian processes, we can derive novel applications to noisy data on a graph, especially those that require smoothness as a key characteristic. Our study demonstrates that these Gaussian processes can be re-expressed as a determinantal point process, which provides the basis for Bayesian inference and model selection through the use of the Edward2 framework. Through simulated data and real-world experiments, our model exhibits a clear advantage over alternative methods used for smooth Gaussian processes. Our approach can be particularly beneficial for creating models that incorporate prior knowledge about a graph's structure.

The optimal detection of road systems in metropolitan areas is a significant problem that can be addressed through a leader-follower game. In this paper, we model the leader as a road system operator seeking to identify the structure of a metropolitan area's road system by sending vehicles with varying levels of observation capabilities. The follower represents a group of vehicles being observed and trying to conceal their path. The road system can be considered detected when the leader's knowledge exceeds a certain threshold based on the observed vehicles. We develop an algorithm to determine the most efficient subset of vehicles required to accurately identify the road system's structure. Furthermore, we explore the impact of varying vehicle observation capabilities on the optimal solution. In practice, this problem can be applied to the optimization of routing systems with partial information.

Our research delves into the impact of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter on the effective field theory of neutrino and dark energy. By analyzing J/ψ decay branching ratios, we investigate how a certain amount of the decay goes undetected. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we explore the significance of detecting these undetected particles through J/ψ spectrum analysis and global neutrino parameters. Our findings indicate that with 10 billion J/ψ events, the level of undetected particles at 5σ detection significance is notable, posing a challenge in understanding the neutrino efficient field theory. Additionally, we discover that the amount of undetected particles can be as high as 10^-3, which may imply a connection between dark matter and the J/ψ invisible decay. Therefore, identifying the nature of the J/ψ invisible decay is crucial in determining the parameters of the efficient field theory of neutrino and dark energy.

Second-order differential equation-based systems can be solved using the SDIMSIM method, which applies variable timesteps to achieve efficiency. Traditionally, this method requires equal timesteps. By allowing variable timesteps, the method can be optimized for better accuracy and speed. In this work, we demonstrate that the method can be derived from a mathematical expansion based on variable timesteps. We then develop a new, simplified algorithm for variable timestep applications. Additionally, we show that the method can be made more robust by incorporating a stability analysis, which helps in determining appropriate timestep sizes. We also examine the method's convergence properties and how they relate to the choice of timestep sizes. Our results indicate that the method can provide accurate solutions for a range of test problems, even with challenging nonlinear systems. Furthermore, we find that the method can offer significant improvements in computational efficiency compared to the traditional equal-timestep approach.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) as a unified framework that encompasses a wide range of multivariate time series analysis methods, including general SSA, singular spectrum analysis (SSA), and recent extensions such as multivariate SSA and functional SSA. Building on the foundation of individual components, we develop a comprehensive framework for MFSSA, addressing key challenges related to the dimensionality of data, the optimization of the diagonalization method, and the identification of dominant components. Through a structured approach to dimensionality reduction, characterized by the presence or absence of the "tensor" label, we provide a clear roadmap for researchers to choose between alternative dimensions. Furthermore, we propose a novel diagnostic tool for dimensionality reduction, known as the singular spectrum difference (SSD), in conjunction with MFSSA. Through a series of simulated scenarios and real-world applications, we demonstrate the effectiveness of MFSSA, in addition to an R package called "MFSSA" to facilitate the implementation of MFSSA methods.

In recent times, significant interest has emerged in the AutoML Ensemble Methods, particularly their potential to address tasks such as classification, regression, and ranking. In response to these developments, researchers have begun creating suites of nested experiments to compare and evaluate various ensemble methods. One such suite is the Advanced Ensemble Study (AES), designed to investigate seven essential aspects of ensemble methods and has been implemented across three distinct datasets and three different test conditions. Our analysis of the AES framework reveals that it suffers from two key issues: a lack of robustness due to an over-reliance on positive results and an excessive sensitivity to the random sampling of data used for training and validation. In an effort to address these limitations and provide accurate assessments of ensemble methods, we propose a range of methodological refinements, including more rigorous statistical testing, the use of performance-based cohort selection, and a revised framework for evaluating ensemble methods that prioritizes practical applications. Through our modified AES framework, we have conducted additional experiments to gauge the performance of state-of-the-art ensemble methods on a range of classification tasks. Our findings include the observation that simple ensemble methods such as Bagging and Forest Multiple Output Classifiers consistently excel over more complex alternatives, and our proposed approach is poised to yield more reliable and valid conclusions in the evaluation of AutoML Ensemble Methods.

This paper examines the time a stochastic process spends within a predetermined distance of its initial value, before considering the full path the process takes. Typically, results only account for time spent exactly on the starting point, but our research extends this to include time spent on either side of the origin, providing lower and upper time estimates. The time spent on one side of the origin is compared to a persistent random walk's time spent on the starting point, while the time spent on the other side is compared to a regular random walk's time spent on that point.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma generator with a 1-meter length and 0.4-meter diameter provides the plasma necessary for these experiments. Operated by a 13.56 MHz RF power source, the generator features a helicon-type antenna that produces a plasma plasma plume extending 0.5 meters into the vacuum chamber. To optimize plasma conditions, a range of diagnostic tools including Langmuir probes, interferometry, and a spectrometer have been implemented to thoroughly characterize the plasma. The results show that, in helicon mode, the plasma exhibits key characteristics including a critical density of approximately 1.8 x 10^11 cm^-3, an electron temperature around 2.5 eV, and a density that can be adjusted between 1 x 10^11 and 2 x 10^12 electrons per cubic centimeter using the generator's power source. The findings also indicate that the plasma uniformity is satisfactory for the IShTAR experiments, and further improvements to the generator's performance are expected with the upgrade to a more powerful 40 kW RF source.

The model presented in this work simulates the interaction between plants, pathogens, and beneficial microorganisms to illustrate the potential of using microorganisms as a pesticide. The model is based on system dynamics and consists of three key components: plant, pathogen, and beneficial microorganism. The model explores different victim quantities where the pathogen preys on the plant and is attacked by the beneficial microorganism in a closed system. When the pathogen quantity exceeds a certain threshold, the model demonstrates that the beneficial microorganism is able to effectively manage the pest through appropriate control methods, including exploitation, displacement, and manipulation of the environment. The model also shows the impact of various victim quantities on the stability of the system.

This study presents a novel nucleus segmentation approach for histopathological tissue samples. The proposed W-Net is a two-stage convolutional network that enhances the performance of simple methods through iterative refinement. The W-Net consists of an initial coarse-stage and a subsequent fine-stage, with each stage utilizing a separate nucleus feature extractor. The coarse-stage reduces noise and incorporates a background suppression module to correct misidentifications. The fine-stage refines the output from the previous stage and corrects local errors. The W-Net shows superior results compared to state-of-the-art methods in nucleus segmentation.

The converse Artin-Rees property is a local cohomological property recently introduced by Huneke and with broader implications than the original Artin-Rees property. This paper focuses on investigating which groups of the form G_{q} (= SO_{q}(n+d), O_{q}(n+d), or Sp_{q}(n+d)) possess the converse Artin-Rees property for their first extension sheaf Lambda^{d}M_{q} in the category of G_{q}-modules. By examining the structure of these groups and utilizing the properties of quantum groups, we are able to prove that the odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups meet this criterion when the parameter q has a specific form (i.e., q is a non-zero element satisfying a particular condition). The same analysis also yields evidence that the converse Artin-Rees property is enjoyed by the classical analogues of these groups (i.e., their limits as the parameter q approaches a specific value).

A graph G is considered to have an iterated line graph l^i(G) that can be detected, where detection capability denotes the ability to identify l^i(G) through a simple visual inspection, whereas an undetectable graph cannot. Furthermore, a graph G is classified as having a hamiltonian pathway index of 1, denoted as hpi(G) = 1, if a hamiltonian path exists in G. In this study, we aim to examine the relationship between detectable iterated line graphs and those with a hamiltonian pathway index of 1. Specifically, we prove that an iterated line graph l^i(G) is detectable if and only if it satisfies the condition hpi(l^i(G)) = 1. Additionally, we provide a new method for constructing hamiltonian paired graphs, thereby extending the previously established connection between detectable iterated line graphs and hamiltonian paired graphs.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to SARS-CoV-2 transmission by facilitating viral spread. Pyroptosis is initiated through two main pathways, involving NLRP3 and caspase-1, or through the direct action of gasdermin B. Once initiated, pyroptosis triggers a self-amplifying reaction that leads to extensive cell damage. This study develops a mathematical model to simulate this self-amplifying reaction and examines the effects of anti-inflammatory interventions on pyroptosis-induced cell death. Our results indicate that interventions targeting the NLRP3 and caspase-1 pathway are more effective than those targeting the gasdermin B pathway. Additionally, we find that in some cases, the NLRP3 pathway's role in pyroptosis can be negligible, and that the gut's lymphoid tissue and the respiratory system have distinct susceptibility patterns. Our model also predicts that in some scenarios, delaying anti-inflammatory treatment can reduce pyroptosis-induced cell death.

In reinforcement learning, external state variables are additional pieces of information used to make decisions, often incorporating a different perspective on the environment. This work delves into the benefits of simplifying RL agents by removing these extra state variables, potentially leading to more efficient and effective solutions. It also explores the potential for indirect benefit by simplifying the environment itself. A key observation made is the overlap between external state variables and incentives provided to the agent, with the proposal to distinguish between these concepts. It is proposed that only variables directly impacting the agent's actions should be included in the state, with other information being used to design a more effective environment for evaluation purposes. A theoretical analysis is performed to examine the feasibility of this approach, with a scenario modeled using multi-task reinforcement learning. Empirical evaluation is conducted across various complex scenarios, including multi-agent scenarios and large-scale navigation tasks, to demonstrate the benefits of this approach in practice. The results show improved performance, reduced complexity, and increased transparency when the approach is applied. The benefits of the approach are also found to generalize across different evaluation metrics and robustness is demonstrated in scenarios with significant disturbances. The work concludes by highlighting potential applications and areas for further research.

A blockchain-based smart contract platform like Tezos can be sophisticatedly validated using refinement types, a logical framework that checks the specificity of types based on their underlying properties. By combining refinement types with dependent types, programmers can accurately express constraints related to numeric values, hash functions, and more. In this presentation, we'll demonstrate how a tool like HELMHOLTZ can effectively identify errors in a user's code by using a combination of refinement and dependent types. This tool can be seen as an upgraded version of the existing type checker found in the Tezos compiler, and its capabilities will be showcased through various code examples that clearly illustrate its advantages. Additionally, we'll explore some complex scenarios where HELMHOLTZ's unique features offer better performance compared to the baseline compiler.

Deep Neural Networks have achieved remarkable performance in various image and signal processing tasks. Recent advancements in neural networks have led to the development of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks, which have been successfully applied to unstructured and structured data. GCNNs leverage neural network technology to detect patterns in data, but its underlying mechanism remains unclear compared to traditional neural networks. This paper lays out a matched filtering approach to break down a GCNN into its fundamental components, providing insight into its working principles and matching the neural network's parameterization from first principles.

We investigate a novel Chern-Simons theory, based on a novel composite connection, which generates a gravity system linked to a scalar field and gauge fields. This framework mirrors Einstein-Hilbert action along with a Weyl-Minkowski action, utilizing a Chern-Simons term that relates to a conformal transformation. Our primary objective is to analyze static, asymptotically flat black holes and solitons within this Chern-Simons gravity framework, considering both electric and magnetic charges. The solution for this system can be found by transforming the conformally flat metric into a Weyl metric, which allows us to determine the mass, electric and magnetic charges, based on the Chern-Simons term. This term ensures that hairy black holes and solitons meet the positivity principle. We then examine the stability of these solutions through a linearized fluctuation analysis, discovering that spinning black holes and solitons can be hairy. Moreover, we find that both electric and magnetic charges can end a graviton, gravitino or a fermion zero-mode.

The proposed concept of non-reversible algebra simplifies to a well-known theoretical concept when applied to physical systems. Specifically, it relates to polynomial algebras that are non-degenerate when the flow of time is reversed. A key characteristic of non-reversible algebras is the presence of branes within the context of string theory, allowing for the realization of non-reversible algebras as boundary symmetries. A brane configuration corresponding to a non-reversible algebra has been identified for the W-algebra specific example. Furthermore, the connection between branes and the anti-involutions of non-reversible algebras has been established, leading to a deeper understanding of branes through the reflection of non-reversible algebras' properties.

Elastography, an advanced imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathology by identifying the mechanical properties of tissues. It relies on accurate estimation of tissue displacement in different ultrasound frames following the induction of tissue deformation. The performance of elastography is hinderedly by limited field-of-view and lateral shift issues. The issue of limited field-of-view is addressed by increasing the scanning depth of the ultrasound transmitter and modifying the receiver's perspective. However, the challenge of lateral shift remains unresolved. The Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique was explored as a potential solution to the issue of lateral shift. In VOSA, the virtual origin is moved laterally to compensate for the limited field-of-view. It was hypothesised that VOSA would enhance the performance of lateral shift estimation. To test this hypothesis, numerical simulations and ultrasound elastography experiments were conducted. The results of these experiments confirmed the potential of VOSA to enhance the performance of lateral shift estimation. It was also demonstrated that VOSA outperformed the conventional synthetic aperture technique in scenarios where tissues with different mechanical properties are present. These findings suggest that VOSA can be integrated with ultrasound elastography to improve its accuracy.

This guide is intended for students who have encountered basic algorithms concepts but need further explanation on how they work. It provides detailed, non-technical explanations of popular algorithms, using clear examples to illustrate each step. The focus is on presenting the'spirit' of an algorithm through simple examples, rather than a formal mathematical derivation, and the resulting resource can be a useful companion to standard computer science textbooks.

We investigate how a set of posets known as V-shaped posets behaves in relation to the Ramsey property, specifically within the context of Boolean structures. Our analysis focuses on various characteristics of these posets, such as their size, the distance between their highest elements, and whether they have a certain minimal element, and determines the minimum number of colors required to guarantee that any mapping between them contains a monochromatic V-shaped substructure. This is true under the assumption that these posets contain at least three elements.

In the context of large-scale high-dimensional data, a significant challenge arises when attempting to identify meaningful clusters by applying the standard $k$-means algorithm. This issue becomes particularly pronounced as the number of data points grows in proportion to or faster than the square of the number of clusters. To address this, we introduce a new dynamic $k$-means algorithm that efficiently reduces the impact of high-dimensional coordinates by scaling down the effect of each individual coordinate. This is achieved by modifying the traditional $k$-means update rule to incorporate a learning rate that is directly proportional to the inverse of the square root of the number of data points. This results in significantly improved performance compared to a baseline dynamic $k$-means algorithm, especially noticeable when the data is embedded in a high-dimensional Euclidean space. To further examine the theoretical benefits of our proposed algorithm, we establish an information-theoretic lower bound that demonstrates its optimal scaling with regards to both the number of clusters and data points. This is accompanied by a superior empirical analysis showcasing the algorithm's superior clustering capabilities in comparison to alternative methods.

We introduce a new framework for cooperative games involving stochastic dynamic systems, where agents face uncertainty and a deadline. Our model builds upon the traditional Pursuit-Withdrawal game and is characterized by a hierarchical structure, where agents can differentiate into two distinct groups based on their ability to observe the system's state. We establish a key theorem identifying the optimal cooperative strategy as a closed-form solution, and this involves solving a specific set of Linear Differential Games. To demonstrate the practical applications of our framework, we apply it to the solution of matrix games with a stochastic environment, as well as the control of a system with multiple interconnected subsystems.

A likelihood function that is in circular form can still provide a unique estimate for the model parameters, even when it is not necessarily nontransitive. The condition of being nontransitive actually imposes additional constraints on the parameters, making certain circular likelihood functions ineffective as a means of estimating the parameters. We offer a new classification for likelihood functions that is based on their lack of transitivity and demonstrate that the standard Bayesian approach is effective in identifying the parameters in a context where the likelihood function is both circular and nontransitive. We also examine various alternative methods of estimating the parameters and show that they can be vulnerable to the issues of transitivity.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the current applications of cycleGANs are limited by their inability to switch between the adversarial and non-adversarial training modes, which severely hinders their potential for real-world medical image enhancement. To address this issue, a new cycleGAN architecture is proposed that simultaneously enables mode switching and preserves the unsupervised and distance metric learning characteristics, ultimately resulting in enhanced and realistic high-dose images from low-dose images. The proposed method is evaluated using 900 CT images from 300 patients and shows significant improvements over existing cycleGANs and noise reduction techniques like NLM and DNN.

Continuously acquiring high-quality human labels for dialog comprehension remains a challenge due to the need for detailed content understanding and the ability to recognize what is relevant. To address this issue, a semi-supervised pre-training method is proposed that begins with limited labeled data and extensive unlabeled dialog conversations. A tree-structured classifier is used to efficiently utilize a large amount of unlabeled data by learning a contrastive pre-training objective from paired dialog contexts. This method is tested on the Dialog Semantics Evaluation Dataset, a recently introduced dataset that assesses semantic understanding in dialog, and it outperforms other baseline methods, particularly those that rely solely on labeled data, in a fully supervised setting. Moreover, it demonstrates comparable performance to fully supervised pre-training on the same dataset.

This research introduces a new geometric framework that combines harmonic and soliton principles within the context of an ideal fluid spacetime. By assuming a one-form $\varphi$ and a vector field $X$, we establish a relationship between conformal Yamabe solitons and the ideal fluid spacetime's Ricci-Yamabe soliton. This relationship is expressed as a soliton equation that can be expanded in a local form. Furthermore, we define a conformal Yamabe soliton as a conformal class of the ideal fluid spacetime's Ricci-Yamabe soliton. Additionally, we show that conformal Ricci-Yamabe solitons can be expressed in terms of a harmonic class and a Kashiwada soliton.

To study the distortion effect on rotating halo nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method in a deformed oscillator potential. By adjusting a certain parameter and maintaining other conditions constant, we found that the inertial properties of $^{36}$S and $^{42}$Mg could be analyzed for deformed and und deformed configurations. Our research reveals that for nuclei with large deformations, the distortion has a noticeable influence, whereas for those with minor deformations, the influence is negligible. To separate the distortion and angular momentum effects, we introduced an und deformed oscillator potential with an adjusted parameter. By comparing the results, we found that an und deformed potential can roughly replicate the effects of distortion on inertial properties. However, further research is needed to fully comprehend the influence of distortion on rotating halo nuclei.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and multi-feature alignment to achieve realistic upscaling. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a more advanced alignment technique, while also introducing a new bidirectional frame reinforcement learning strategy. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with source codes and extensive evaluation available online.

This study aims to enhance the efficient estimation of vector boson collisions at extremely high muon energies using kinematic constraints and neural networks. By utilizing a large dataset simulated with the GLASMA generator, our optimal model achieves a 99.975% accuracy in distinguishing between Higgs and Drell-Yan processes occurring at 14 TeV proton-proton collisions producing muons with energies ranging from 100 to 1000 GeV per muon. Furthermore, our model exhibits comparable performance even with limited dataset sizing, resulting in reduced estimates of 97.385% Higgs and 97.387% Drell-Yan process accuracy at 100 GeV per muon and 99.934% Higgs and 99.936% Drell-Yan process accuracy at 1000 GeV per muon.

In complex reinforcement learning systems with multiple tasks, efficient training often relies on a modular approach that leverages a shared abstract representation, such as a world model, to facilitate coordination and learning across tasks. We demonstrate that by using a shared modular representation, reinforcement learning agents can minimize the negative impact of catastrophic interference when training on a series of tasks. We develop a theoretical framework explaining how a world model can mitigate catastrophic forgetting through the use of a task-specific factorization, and subsequently design a series of multi-task reinforcement learning experiments that validate our findings. Our results show that in scenarios with high interference and diverse tasks, a world model-trained system achieves significantly lower memory losses and maintains higher memory performance compared to a single-task trained system. We further investigate several key factors influencing the degree of catastrophic forgetting in multi-task reinforcement learning settings and discover that the choice of representation, memory mechanism, and learning protocol all play vital roles. To further scale up our evaluation, we introduce a suite of 30 related memory tasks within the MultiTask-Procgen game environment, which we make publicly available for future research. Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of modular reinforcement learning as a solution to catastrophic forgetting and showcases its potential to tackle a wide range of memory-intensive reinforcement learning applications.

This paper investigates local approximation schemes for the porous medium type and swift diffusion type equations on a finite noncompact metric measure space with a compact boundary. We first establish a new Harnack type inequality for the superlinear fast diffusion equation in the context of a noncompact open set. We then utilize this result to develop a new uniform gradient approximation for a wide range of nonlinear diffusion equations on a noncompact open set. Furthermore, we provide a global approximation for a wide range of nonlinear diffusion equations on a bounded noncompact open set.

Twenty-five years ago, in 1998, the first Godelian phenomenon was identified - a binary operation on the integers that is one-to-one with respect to each individual integer, yet fails to maintain this property when considering all integers simultaneously. Since this discovery, various Godelian properties have been developed and their underlying causes studied. This article examines four influential logicians from the past, Kurt Godel, Alfred Tarski, Rudolf Carnap, and Joseph Rosser, and how their collective work contributed to understanding these pervasive patterns. Their legacy continues to shape current research in areas like computability theory, model theory, and recursion theory.

This one-dimensional extension of the three-spheres theorem was originally proposed by T. Takahashi in 1984. Using careful differentiation, we reestablish the proposal in a more general setting of hypercomplex functions.

The exponential growth of mobile device location data demands efficient sampling methods to mimic the original distribution while protecting privacy and ensuring security. Current techniques face challenges in handling three key factors: spatial heterogeneity (variations in distribution across space), anisotropy (irregular sampling patterns), and equilibrium (maintaining the same characteristics as the original data). Existing approaches either overlook these constraints or resort to expensive and time-consuming optimization methods. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel, easy-to-implement technique for sampling location data that takes into account spatial heterogeneity, anisotropy, and equilibrium. By leveraging a quadratic mean difference metric, this method facilitates highly efficient and robust learning of models from sampled data. Comprehensive experiments validate the performance benefits of this technique across various models and scenarios.

In our study, we sought to enhance the training of robotic tasks involving an eye-in-hand camera by supplementing sparse teaching scenarios with additional instructional images. Our approach allows for the use of multiple training pictures per task and has been effectively utilized in conjunction with sparse positive feedback training methods. We tested the efficacy of our approach by comparing the performance of robots trained with and without additional images. The results showed that training with additional images yields significantly better outcomes. To further evaluate the benefits and limitations of our approach, we conducted a series of experiments under various lighting conditions and found that the benefits of training with images are most pronounced in low-light environments.

Solving inverse problems involves recovering a initial condition based on the output of a partial differential equation due to the problem's ill-posed nature. Traditional regularization methods are often effective in recovering the initial condition but have limitations in modeling realistic scenarios. In contrast, learning-based approaches can effectively capture complex data patterns, but struggle with stability. To address this issue, we propose a novel regularization strategy for conditional GANs, utilizing a regularization term that enforces coherence with the given data, especially effective in recovering complex initial conditions from limited and noisy measurements. To overcome the issue of forward evaluation of PDEs for sampling, we introduce a reverse sampling technique that generates realistic outputs when given a specific initial condition. Our framework is demonstrated through the inversion of the 1D Burgers equation, showing improved performance compared to existing techniques and strategies.

This study examines the existence of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems of non-integral order. By leveraging the $C$-condition and by drawing upon the functionality of the fractional order derivative, we demonstrate that in a neighborhood of the origin, there are no surfaces invariant to a fractional order system subject to the condition that the fractional order is stable and positive. Additionally, the article discusses the implications of this finding for fractional order Lotka-Volterra systems.

Next-generation wireless networks will rely heavily on Terahertz communication technologies due to their exceptionally high bandwidth potential. However, implementing strong, frequency-hop transmission systems is crucial to address several THz challenges, including intense attenuation, limited coverage, and the need for very short packet lengths. This study focuses on optimizing a multi-hop transmission protocol by utilizing Machine Learning to make critical decisions related to beam training, but it's essential to note that our work can also be applied to other protocols involving the selection of receive and transmit antennas. A key challenge in developing ML methods is the extremely large possible outcome landscape resulting from the combination of a large number of antennas and weak correlations between them. To tackle this issue, we propose an initial two-tier ML framework, in which the outer layer is responsible for identifying the most effective frequency-hop connections and the inner layer is optimized to locate the best beam directions for each individual connection. A key achievement of this study is the derivation of an approximate analytical solution for the optimal multi-hop protocol by leveraging the properties of special ML outcomes, in which the outer layer's choices align with the inner layer's preferences, thus allowing the inner layer to focus on more critical decisions. To validate the efficacy of the proposed framework, we also develop a method for training the ML models and conduct extensive simulations to compare the performance of the optimal multi-hop protocol, along with two-tier ML and a baseline approach that involves a fixed number of frequency-hop connections and beam directions. The results show that the optimal multi-hop protocol

The interstellar medium's scattering properties varies regionally due to the structure of the interstellar medium, thus observing scintillation patterns of pulsars can provide valuable information about the scattering regions. This work presents statistical analysis of B1133+16's single-pulse data from 1993 to 2000, utilizing a high-sensitivity telescope at Urumqi, and reveals that the scintillation pattern changes over time are more pronounced in higher-resolution data, indicating the presence of multiple components in the pulsar's line of sight. A three-dimensional model was then constructed to fit the scintillation pattern parameters, revealing that the scattering geometry is aligned with the local interstellar magnetic field in the solar neighborhood and that the pulsar is about 4.2 parsecs away from a prominent HII region named the Pipe Nebula. The findings of this work have implications for the study of regional variations in the interstellar medium.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network is modified to incorporate external pitch input via a novel technique involving dilated convolution layers that adapt their sampling rates dynamically. Secondly, a cascaded network structure is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies separately with distinct dilated convolution layers. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate superior results in terms of mean opinion score (MOS) and log mel frequency cepstral distance (LMFCD) compared to the baseline WaveNet and other models.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction platform for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. The developed framework
facilitates morphological annotation and spelling correction by utility tools, data
exploration, and collaborative features. Additionally, access to external knowledge
sources, such as dictionaries and grammatical rules, has been integrated via
APIs/linking to Benedict and LEMLA dictionaries. A case study is also described,
involving the annotation of dialectal texts, along with a technical overview of the
system's architecture.

As exoplanets are discovered at an incredible rate, it's now feasible to study planets across various categories, including those suitable for life and planets with atmospheric systems that could aid in maintaining life on their surface. This study delves into the chemical interactions between these exoplanets' atmospheres and their host stars' energy emissions. We examine how different star types alter the photochemical processes in these atmospheres, focusing on planets surrounded by dense atmospheres in front of G-K dwarfs. These atmospheres are only partially affected by photochemical changes, leaving room for biological molecules such as OCPs to form beneath layers of gas. However, their outer regions likely contain significant amounts of oxygen-based molecules like O2, OH, and H2O due to photochemical breakdown of biomass-generated CH4. As a result, existing or future telescopes observing these planets in the visible to near-infrared spectra may be able to identify signs of biological life but it would require sufficient atmospheric density or sufficient cooling to prevent photochemical degradation. Additionally, we discuss how future missions like HabEx and CHAOS could find evidence of life on these planets by analyzing their starlight.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling may also become impeded by heat-generated defects in the high-resistance lead, further setting it apart from the signature of a Majorana state.

The development of advanced, efficient, and secure highway infrastructure poses a significant challenge for civil engineers. To tackle this issue, a novel framework called RoadAtlas is introduced, with the aim of automating highway inspection and maintenance operations. This framework leverages machine learning and deep learning techniques to identify anomalies and defects in highway surfaces from video data captured using unmanned aerial vehicles. Furthermore, RoadAtlas includes a data platform that enables real-time asset tracking and management across large areas. The performance of RoadAtlas was evaluated through a case study involving the inspection of a 10-kilometer highway section, and the results showed a 70% reduction in inspection costs and a 50% decrease in time required for data analysis.

The concept of shadows has recently been introduced as a measure for assessing the visibility of edges in graph embeddings. This study expands the realm of shadows to encompass a broader range of spatial representations, known as bicategorical embeddings, which involve mapping graph vertices to the points of a surface and assigning edges to the surfaces' regions corresponding to their connections. By extrapolating the principles of classical visibility to these new spatial mappings, the concept of bicategorical shadows is formulated. A key contribution of this research is the development of shadow-computing algorithms for various surface types, including 2D polygons and spherical triangles. Furthermore, a shadow-scoring system is introduced, scoring the information content of a graph based on its shadow-casting embeddings, which is shown to be useful in analyzing the network's topological structure. This research is relevant to areas like information theory, topology, and computer graphics.

Estimating the location of sound sources is a critical function that is dependent on visual and auditory cues as well as prior knowledge. Our primary sensory input for localizing sounds originates from binaural differences in the time of arrival and interaural phase differences. Although machine learning models can accurately predict front/rear classification from these cues, they tend to perform much worse when trying to estimate elevation. Our research aims to enhance the training of elevation classification models by introducing two new datasets that utilize raw audio inputs. We also explore various features that these models can use, including extracting features from the raw audio itself. The findings reveal that using audio features yields significant performance improvements over traditional approaches that rely on time difference and phase difference features. Notably, our research discovers that convolutional neural networks trained on elevation classification tasks can achieve class-wise generalization, even in the absence of label noise, suggesting that the limitations we encountered were self-imposed. By removing restrictions on data labeling, we find that ML models can achieve elevation classification accuracy of over 70% using audio features.

Current Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operate within a fixed undirected and unweighted framework, but real-world networks often exhibit directionality and non-uniform edge weights. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel class of neural networks called Lorentzian GNNs, characterized by their ability to effectively handle positive and non-zero edge weights within a directed graph setting. Lorentzian GNNs are underpinned by a unique differentiable matrix exponential formula that maintains directional edge weight properties during message passing. We leverage this capability to develop two distinct models: Directional Temporal GCN for temporal prediction tasks and Weighted Multi-Task Lorentzian GNN for multi-task learning. Experimental results across multiple datasets reveal significant enhancements in performance compared to existing GNN methods. Our work provides a crucial step in enhancing the practicality and scalability of GNNs for real-world applications.

This study seeks to address an inverse problem in a specific structural acoustic context. We aim to recover either the source term or the damping coefficient within a particular structure, given certain conditions applied to an adjacent acoustic space.

In optomechanics, mechanically induced squeezing in a mirror can be used to create a non-classical state of light. Typically, this process requires a highly efficient conversion from mechanical energy to optical squeezing. In a hybrid system that combines optical and mechanical modes, we investigate the possibility of achieving stable optical squeezing through a process called parametric amplification. Our analysis shows that by selecting appropriate parameters, optical squeezing can be generated even if the mechanical oscillator is over-damped, a scenario that usually hinders squeezing generation. Furthermore, our findings indicate that optical squeezing can be transmitted over long distances with minimal loss, making this approach suitable for distributed quantum information processing.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to sets represented as tuples, akin to the approach used in propositional dynamic logic with cooperation. Our investigation focuses on two key dimensions: whether the model allows for the intersection of programs (corresponding to the union of their interpretations) and whether the variables in the formula are grouped as either individual entities or as part of a larger unit. Our analysis reveals that the most expressive category is $\mu\sigma\mu$-calculus, which enables the combination of programs and the grouping of variables. We also explore the relationship between this complexity and the presence of bailiffs in modal $\mu$-calculus, finding that the two are equivalent in terms of their expressive power.

This paper presents a new exponential delay devaluation model inspired by the Tsallis distribution, offering a theoretical framework that builds upon the foundation established by the 2021 paper 'The Exponential Delay Devaluation (EDD) Model: A Rethink of the Rational Choice Theory'. The EDD model's current limitation in adhering to Ebert's condition for extended periods is acknowledged. In contrast, the proposed Tsallis-inspired model demonstrates a more sustainable level of preference persistence. The new model's exceptional relevance is shown through its application to a realistic scenario, predicting the outcomes of a competitive game scenario. Furthermore, the model's parameters are estimated using real-world data from a survey conducted in Hong Kong, and a comparative analysis is performed to validate its superiority over the original EDD model.

In our previous theory called Heavy Gravity, we introduced a novel concept, harmonic gauge, which is distinct from the conventional gauge used in general relativity. This harmonic gauge in Heavy Gravity remains unaltered even with the presence of highly dense objects that distort space-time. As a result, we were able to derive a simplified and explicit formula for gravitational waves without the usual high-dimensional tensor components, which are typically obscured by the intense gravitational field. In this paper, we further explore the characteristics of heavy gravity by examining how it is affected by a rotating neutron star in a binary system. Using numerical simulations, we determined the precise range in which the gravitational frequency remains harmonic, and found that even in heavy gravity, the gravitational wave frequency follows the general relativistic relationship f = (11.0 ± 0.1)np/N, where np represents the neutron star's rotation rate and N denotes the number of solar masses of the neutron star. This harmonic behavior is seen in high-frequency waves generated by the neutron star's internal structure, but is instead dominated by the neutron star's external geometry in low-frequency waves. Additionally, our findings align with the predictions made by researchers using other approaches, such as the post-Newtonian method, within a specific range.

A signed graph is a pair consisting of an undirected graph and a function assigning signs to its edges. This concept can be interpreted through the lens of Coxeter systems, specifically by applying the Birkhoff-Lewis theorem to extend the notion of a cover to a broader category of objects, including covers of Coxeter systems. Furthermore, this approach enables the creation of a new concept, the expanded double cover of a Coxeter system, which can be viewed as a cover of a modified version of the original system.

In the Weyl-Wigner representation, phase and coordinate spaces are intertwined, allowing for the representation of classical statistical mechanics within a quantum framework. By examining the canonical ensemble in this context, we derive a detailed, operator-based representation of thermal equilibrium conditions, incorporating an operator version of Liouville's theorem. Additionally, we show that in the Weyl-Wigner representation, the canonical density operator corresponds to a coherent state operator, thereby providing a physical interpretation of thermal equilibrium within this quantum regime.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has been widely recognized as a legitimate physical phenomenon over the past decade, since its first introduction in 2003. Initially, it was considered novel, as it challenged traditional perceptions of temperature. Tutorials and comprehensive analyses have since been conducted to fully grasp its advantages and applications. Despite these achievements, several key aspects of negative temperature remain unclear and in need of further clarification. In this presentation, we will address the embedding of negative temperature within the broader context of negative and infinite energy levels. A previously developed model will be reviewed to illustrate the complexities of negative temperature in quantum systems. Key challenges in implementing negative temperature in quantum states will be identified, along with the consequences of level nonorthogonality. Finally, the interconnection between negative temperature, nonhermitian quantum mechanics, and bi-hermitian quantum mechanics will be explored.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a partial sum of A to the power h, denoted as $s_h(A)$. The constrained sum of A to the power h, denoted as $S_h(A)$, consists of all possible values of $s_h(A)$. In this study, we aim to determine the minimum number of elements in A, denoted as |A|, required to guarantee that $S_h(A)$ contains all possible values in a specific range. We establish upper and lower limits for |A| in the case of integer subsets. Specifically, if A is a set of integers with a sum of zero, we can find an upper limit for $S_h(A)$ as $2^{2h-2}|A|-1$ and a lower limit as $2^{2h-1}|A|-1$ for most values of h. Furthermore, we demonstrate various techniques to achieve both the upper and lower limits in certain scenarios. However, it remains challenging to determine a lower limit for |A| in some cases, leading to an open question. This study is an extension of previous research on the constrained sum of pairs, introducing new sumset inequalities and novel proof methods.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically to determine cancer risk potential and guide patient treatment requires precise pathological evaluation. Despite the importance of these features, there is currently a lack of standardization in their description. To address this shortcoming, we propose a comprehensive dataset of annotated histopathological images of colorectal polyps, along with associated clinical information. This collection, called UniToPatho, comprises 3,522 images (1,042 polyps with associated clinical information and 2,480 used for training and validation) from 62 different pathologists. It serves as a standard for describing polyp histopathology and provides a set of training and validation images for doctors in residency and a dataset for developing machine learning algorithms dedicated to classifying polyps and determining the severity of adenomas.

This research proposes an adjustable finite element method for solving time-harmonic diffusion equations that involves manipulating the original diffusion matrix. The spectrum of the stiffness matrix is shifted through an ill-conditioned transformation to facilitate iterative solvers in frequency domain problems, particularly those with slowly varying coefficients. A novel, straightforward approach is presented for determining an optimal matrix adjustment, minimizing forward and inverse conditioning at each iteration. A more exotic alternative method is also examined, using a quasi-orthogonal basis to create a diagonally dominant stiffness matrix. Both strategies are compared, and the advantages of adjusting the stiffness matrix are highlighted through numerical experiments, demonstrating improved convergence rates and reduced memory requirements in comparison to standard finite element methods.

We are providing an updated analysis of a previous finding, based on measurements of water content in Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites. Previous research suggested that planetesimals in the inner solar system possessed a significantly higher water level, approximately 10 times more than outer planetesimals. This study offers a new approach using multiple measurements, incorporating petrologic and textural factors that may have contributed to varying water levels within individual meteorites. By controlling for these factors, we applied a statistical method to eliminate their influence. The study reveals that even with control for petrologic and textural variables, there is still a notable difference in water levels between the inner and outer solar system planetesimals. To explain this, we considered several factors, including how short-range aliphatic water chains affect the binding force between silicate particles, and how this impact is further significant at lower temperatures typical of the inner solar system. We used a theoretical delivery model of volatile compounds, considering how water content in the solar nebula changed with distance from the Sun, and found that it followed a second-degree polynomial pattern. By controlling for additional variables, we applied a statistical test, and it revealed that water levels in the inner solar system planetesimals are significantly higher than in the outer solar system, at approximately 20 times more.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find the structure factors for the XXZ lattice spin models of ranks higher than one. This result is a generalization of the work by R. Sato for the rank-one XXZ chain. The proposed formula for the structure factors is then verified by comparing their sum with the known thermodynamic data for the high-spin regime, where an exact expression for the low-lying excitation spectrum is derived. Additionally, we establish an affine quantum-group symmetry for the higher-rank XXZ lattice models. This symmetry enables the direct calculation of the structure factors through the quantum-deformed operator-product expansion method. As an example, we compute the one-body correlation function for the XXZ chain with rank two and verify its agreement with the results obtained from the Bethe-ansatz method.

Language models have made significant progress in recent years, boasting impressive performance in various tasks like translation, summarization, and generation. Nonetheless, they fall short when it comes to understanding the meanings of sentences they've never seen before. This limitation holds true for speech, which is even more constrained due to the higher costs associated with data collection. Consequently, speech models lag behind their text-based counterparts in comprehending unfamiliar language. This study sets out to bridge this gap by introducing a novel approach to semantic understanding, one that enables speech and text to be translated into each other automatically. We've applied this approach to both monolithic and transformer-based models, with the results showing our approaches outperform traditional multi-task training methods. Moreover, our methods allow for easy extension to additional tasks like classification and retrieval.

We present a new series expansion for the scattering cross section of any object, based on multipolar coefficients, which are related to the object's electric and magnetic multipole moments. This approach goes beyond the limitations of the long wavelength approximation and provides a foundation for predicting optical tidal forces and spin angular momentum transfer. The validity of this method is demonstrated with examples using a dielectric sphere and a junction, and it is shown that the results can be applied to calculate the optical tidal force and spin angular momentum transfer. Furthermore, we propose a new method for determining the multipolar coefficients directly from measurements of the scattered field, which can be used to study an object's internal properties.

This study introduces three key concepts in its mathematical exploration: quantum immanents, double Young-Capelli bitableaux and Schur altered symmetric functions. The specific focus lies on categorizing double Young-Capelli bitableaux into distinct subgroups based on their properties, specifically whether they generate the same irreducible Schur altered symmetric functions when combined with the quantum immanent. Another area of focus involves describing the entire set of irreducible quantum immanents through the use of a matriux basis linked to the alternating group and examining how these immanents relate to the dual Young-Capelli basis. These concepts also allow for an alternative derivation of altered Schur functions, specifically the primitive ones, when combining the quantum immanent with elements from the group algebra of the symmetric group, particularly through the application of a universal property. This, in turn, leads to a further exploration of the relationship between the irreducible quantum immanents and the primitive Schur altered symmetric functions, ultimately resulting in a demonstration that every primitive Schur altered symmetric function can be expressed as a product of a specific double Young-Capelli bitableaux and a particular irreducible quantum immanent.

We examine a simple scoto-seesaw framework that generates small neutrino masses and creates first-order electroweak baryogenesis through CP-violating and out-of-equilibrium processes. This model includes a minimal set of heavy scalar doublets with distinct CP properties, allowing us to analyze the baryogenesis and dark matter phenomena. With the assistance of a dark sector that involves a minimal set of WIMP-like particles, we find that their present-day dark matter mass is determined by a single parameter that can be pinpointed using baryon asymmetry, thus making it naturally generated. Furthermore, we discover that the vacuum stability of the Higgs field is guaranteed by an inherently large parameter compared to the baryogenesis parameter, which is already satified by a relatively small mass comparison. This results in an extremely constrained parameter space that can be explored in depth. Additionally, we investigate the predicted neutrino masses, direct and indirect dark matter searches, and Higgs decay widths with a specific focus on their sensitivity to the baryogenesis parameter.

We employ the Zaanen vortical functional form to examine the spectral weight of spin waves in orbital-only coupled systems. Utilizing a 180-degree rotation symmetry constraint to restrict possible interactions to either $t_{2g}$ or $e_g$ types, we investigate the spectral weight in both 4d and 5d transition metal compounds. Our analysis highlights the differences in such systems by demonstrating how the spectral weight varies based on the type of orbital, whether it is $t_{2g}$ or $e_g$. Additionally, we offer a least-square minimization method that determines the spectral weight by considering both broadening and rotation symmetry constraints in a self-consistent manner. Our proposed method is compared to existing approaches, and we identify its key benefits, especially when dealing with larger systems or those with intricate electron interactions. Furthermore, we provide a framework for evaluating system electronic properties using this method.

This study examines how relative quantum homology is affected by changing the basis of a symplectic manifold's coordinates. We demonstrate that the shift vectors behave linearly under this change, and subsequently derive formulas for disabled disk classes and the relative quantum potential. Notably, our method is shown to be independent of prior work by Kiem-Thomas in categories other than the Fock-Chen basis.

The accuracy of AI in interpreting chest X-rays is dependent on various factors including the quality of the images used for training and deploying the models. Poor image quality can lead to decreased performance and unreliable results from the AI models. This paper presents a novel convolutional neural network (CNN) that automatically identifies and improves the clarity of abnormal chest X-rays. We experimented with a dataset containing 2,000 chest X-rays with associated quality assessments, training and evaluating our proposed system. The results show that the CNN effectively identifies and enhances the clarity of illneses on chest X-rays.

Reducing high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional representations is a common statistical approach used to visualize and simplify data analysis. There are many established methods for this process, however, achieving optimal results can be challenging and often requires iterative experimentation to find the most effective technique and parameters. To streamline this process, our ViDaExpert tool provides a user-friendly interface for users to set initial parameters, execute dimensionality reduction algorithms, and evaluate the results all within a single, intuitive platform. Available at www.vidaexpert.cz, this tool allows users to import their data, try different dimensionality reduction techniques and evaluation metrics, visualize results, and compare output representations. With ViDaExpert's flexible architecture, new algorithms can be easily integrated into the tool via a separate repository.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over flat regions is a computationally intensive task, especially when done accurately. Our proposed approach simplifies this evaluation, yielding a highly efficient approximation method. By comparing potential values at key points, usually required for image deconvolution, geometric algebra can be used to significantly reduce computational time. Our new method is highly sensitive to changes in input data and outperforms existing techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a challenging test case from an astronomical context. Our method takes substantially less time to compute a related quantity, known as a psf operator, which is essential for solving the problem. Our results show that our method can produce high-quality solutions in a reasonable amount of time.
